nameStory: The 'tun tree' name comes from one of its many common names, 'Chinese toon,' which refers to its mahogany-like wood quality. In its native Asia, it's called 'xiāngchūn' meaning 'fragrant spring' because its young leaves have a distinctive oniony smell and are harvested as a spring vegetable. The colorful nickname 'beef and onion plant' hints at this unique edible quality that makes it stand out from other trees.
description: The tun tree is a medium-sized deciduous tree from Asia that can grow 40-60 feet tall with a rounded crown. It's a member of the mahogany family and has large, compound leaves that can reach over a foot long, made up of many smaller leaflets arranged along a central stem. The tree produces clusters of small, fragrant white flowers in summer, followed by papery seed capsules. What makes this tree truly unique is the strong onion-like smell of its crushed leaves and young shoots.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves up to 18 inches long with 10-20 oval leaflets arranged along a reddish stem. When crushed, they smell strongly of onions or garlic - this scent is unmistakable and immediate.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, creamy white flowers bloom in large, drooping clusters in early summer. Each flower is about 1/4 inch across with 5 petals and has a sweet, pleasant fragrance that contrasts with the oniony leaves.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young becomes furrowed with age, developing long, shallow grooves. The inner bark has a reddish tint that's visible in deeper cuts or damage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Papery brown capsules about an inch long that split open to release winged seeds. The capsules hang in clusters and rattle when shaken, persisting into fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded crown with spreading branches. Young shoots are often reddish and the tree has a somewhat tropical appearance despite being cold-hardy.

habitat: In New England, tun trees are primarily found as landscape specimens in yards, parks, and botanical gardens rather than growing wild. They prefer well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, and are hardy enough to survive New England winters. With only 10 recorded observations in the region, they remain quite rare and are mostly planted by gardeners interested in unusual or edible landscape trees.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with a bronze-red tint before turning green, and young shoots are often harvested for their edible, onion-flavored leaves. The compound leaves unfold relatively late in spring.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage provides dense shade, and fragrant white flower clusters appear in early to mid-summer. This is when the oniony leaf scent is strongest and most noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and papery seed capsules mature and split open. The tree may drop leaves earlier than many native species.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the tree's rounded form and furrowed gray bark. The distinctive compound leaf scars and reddish young twigs can aid in identification.

funFact: In China, the young leaves of tun tree are considered a delicacy and are scrambled with eggs, used in stir-fries, or eaten fresh - they taste like a cross between onions and herbs, and a single tree can provide a family's spring vegetable harvest for weeks!
confusionNotes: The compound leaves might remind you of ash trees or black walnut, but the unmistakable onion smell when crushed immediately sets the tun tree apart. Remember: if it smells like your kitchen garden, it's probably the tun tree!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Chinese cedar,' this tree isn't related to true cedars at all - it's actually in the mahogany family. The 'cedar' name likely comes from its aromatic wood, which was valued for furniture making in Asia, similar to how cedar wood is prized here.
compareHints: As the only Toona species found in New England, compare it instead to other mahogany family members. Unlike the tropical mahoganies you might see in conservatories, tun tree is fully cold-hardy and has that diagnostic onion scent. It's much more aromatic than any of its mahogany relatives and has larger, more numerous leaflets in its compound leaves.
